input.note:
## Root Cause

Kubernetes is not at fault. The crash loop is caused by a **Go runtime panic inside the pricing-engine application itself**, triggered by a bad pricing rule in the rules-admin data store.

---

## Evidence

**Both pods** (`pricing-engine-74d9c6b8f-5tnwh` and `pricing-engine-74d9c6b8f-jq7lc`) show identical crash sequences in their logs:

1. The engine starts and fetches **1,204 active rules from rules-admin at revision 8841**.
2. It attempts to compile rule **`BF-2026-STACKED`** (`tiers=3, stacking=true`).
3. It immediately panics with:
   ```
   panic: runtime error: index out of range [3] with length 3
   github.com/acme/pricing/internal/rules.(*TierTable).Lookup @ tiers.go:88
   ```
4. The process exits with **exit code 2** and Kubernetes restarts it — both pods have hit 12 restarts and are in `CrashLoopBackOff` [cite: concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle#container-restarts-1].

The panic is an **off-by-one error** in `TierTable.Lookup` (`tiers.go:88`): the rule declares `tiers=3`, but the TierTable is 0-indexed (valid indices 0–2), so looking up index 3 goes out of bounds. The pricing-engine image (`4.11.3`, deployed 2026-04-27) has not changed — what changed is the **rules data**: rule `BF-2026-STACKED` appears to have been added or modified in rules-admin around 2 pm today (matching the reported start time), pushing revision 8841.

---

## Fix

There are two steps:

**1. Immediate — restore service:**
Disable or delete rule `BF-2026-STACKED` in the rules-admin UI/API so the pricing-engine can start without encountering the bad rule. Once the rule is gone, the next pod restart will succeed and prices will recover.

**2. Long-term — fix the bug:**
The `TierTable.Lookup` function in `tiers.go:88` does not guard against a caller passing an out-of-bounds tier index. The engineering team should patch the off-by-one error (add a bounds check or convert from 1-based to 0-based correctly before the lookup) and deploy a fixed image before re-enabling any stacked-tier rule with `tiers≥3`.

No Kubernetes configuration changes are needed [cite: concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle#container-restarts-1].
